title: Patent Safe Harbor
description: The patent safe harbor treats a USPTO-issued utility patent as conclusive evidence that research discovered technological information under IRC § 41.
summary: The patent safe harbor under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) treats a USPTO-issued utility patent as conclusive evidence that research discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. It excludes design patents, and taxpayers must still prove the business component, process of experimentation, qualified purpose, and non-funded research requirements.

body.text: The patent safe harbor under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) treats a USPTO-issued utility patent as conclusive evidence that research discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. It excludes design patents, and taxpayers must still prove the business component, process of experimentation, qualified purpose, and non-funded research requirements.
Executive Legal Synthesis and Overview

The Patent Safe Harbor (PSH), codified at Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), is a specialized evidentiary rule governing the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—under Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. or IRC) § 41. Promulgated in final regulations by the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) under T.D. 9104 (69 FR 26, effective January 2, 2004, and applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e)), the provision establishes that the issuance of a patent by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) under 35 U.S.C. § 151—explicitly excluding design patents issued under 35 U.S.C. § 171—constitutes "conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature that is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component". Within the context of an IRS examination, this conclusive presumption removes two technically subjective inquiries under IRC § 41(d) from administrative contention: first, whether the underlying research fundamentally relied on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), and second, whether the taxpayer sought to eliminate technical capability, method, or design uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i).

Despite its considerable utility as an administrative and examination defense mechanism, the Patent Safe Harbor is strictly bounded in regulatory scope and does not establish per se eligibility for the federal R&D tax credit. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for Qualified Research Activities (last updated June 2005) emphasizes, "the issuance of a patent is not conclusive evidence of qualified research, as the taxpayer still has to meet all the other activity requirements of section 41(d)". Specifically, a patent holder must independently substantiate that the research was intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), that "substantially all"—defined under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) as at least 80 percent—of the research activities constituted elements of a systematic process of experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)), and that the experimentation was conducted for a statutorily qualified purpose relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality (IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)). Furthermore, the Patent Safe Harbor operates exclusively at the activity qualification level under IRC § 41(d) and provides no legal protection against expense disallowance under the Funded Research exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)) or the exclusive cost-category limitations of IRC § 41(b). This structural bifurcation between activity qualification and expenditure eligibility creates a second-order compliance hazard wherein corporate taxpayers over-rely on intellectual property grants while neglecting project-level cost accounting and contractual risk allocation.

Primary law under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) and T.D. 9104 restricts the safe harbor strictly to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), which governs discovering technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty.

Second, regarding the patent issuance statutory citation, both the IRS ATG (June 2005) and secondary commentary (Strike Tax) contain a typographical error citing 35 U.S.C. § 51 as the federal patent issuance statute. The governing Treasury regulation at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) and Title 35 of the United States Code confirm that the authoritative statutory citation is 35 U.S.C. § 151 ("Issue of patent"). Within the Internal Revenue Code, IRC § 41(e) governs basic research payments to qualified university and scientific organizations, while 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e) sets forth regulatory effective dates. The Funded Research exclusion is actually codified at IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and implemented through 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3).

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)–(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)–(e), the 65 percent limitation applies only to third-party contract research expenses paid by a hiring taxpayer; a performing contractor whose research is unfunded claims 100 percent of its eligible in-house wage and supply QREs. Sudderth v. Commissioner (Docket No. 37021-21, Feb. 14, 2022) is an unrelated U.S. Tax Court procedural order designating a place of trial; the actual R&D tax credit precedent involving patented technologies, executive wages, and the Four-Part Test is Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework of the Research Credit and the Four-Part Test
Interplay Between IRC § 41 and IRC § 174 / § 174A

Federal tax law incentivizes domestic research and development through two distinct but interlocking statutory regimes: the deduction or amortization of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC § 174 and IRC § 174A, and the incremental tax credit for increasing research activities under IRC § 41. Originally enacted in 1981 and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113), IRC § 41(a)(1) provides a general research credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount.

Because IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) conditions "qualified research" status on whether the underlying expenditures qualify as R&E expenditures, statutory changes to R&E deductibility directly affect the threshold of IRC § 41. Prior to 2022, taxpayers could immediately deduct domestic and foreign R&E expenditures in the year paid or incurred under IRC § 174(a), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) required that qualified research expenditures "may be treated as expenses under section 174". Effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, Section 13206 of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, 131 Stat. 2111) amended IRC § 174 to prohibit immediate deductions and require taxpayers to capitalize "specified research or experimental expenditures" and amortize them ratably over a 5-year period for domestic research (and a 15-year period for foreign research), beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year, while updating IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) to reference "specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174".

Subsequently, under Title VII, Section 70302 of Pub. L. 119-21 (139 Stat. 191, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted July 4, 2025), Congress enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A, which permanently restored immediate expensing—providing that "there shall be allowed as a deduction any domestic research or experimental expenditures which are paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year"—for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Simultaneously, Pub. L. 119-21 amended IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) to define qualified research as research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A," and restricted IRC § 174 (under the statutory text in effect as of July 5, 2026) solely to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which remain subject to mandatory 15-year ratable amortization under IRC § 174(a)(2)(B). Transition provisions under Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(e)–(f) allow eligible small businesses meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test to elect retroactive application of IRC § 174A to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and permit taxpayers to deduct remaining unamortized pre-2025 domestic R&E balances either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a two-taxable-year period. The bifurcated structure created by Pub. L. 119-21 reinforces that foreign R&E expenditures amortized under IRC § 174 cannot enter the IRC § 41 credit base, which is statutorily restricted to domestic research under both IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (via IRC § 174A) and the geographic exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F).
Categories of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) Under IRC § 41(b)

While the Patent Safe Harbor operates at the activity level under IRC § 41(d), the credit calculation itself applies strictly to Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on an existing trade or business under IRC § 41(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1). As the IRS QRE Audit Techniques Guide (updated July 2, 2026) states, IRC § 41(b) establishes an exclusive list: "If an expense is not set forth in section 41(b), a taxpayer may not claim the expense as a QRE". Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2, QREs are divided into in-house research expenses and contract research expenses encompassing four specific expenditure categories.

The first in-house category consists of employee wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d), defined as taxable wages under IRC § 3401(a) (reported on Form W-2, including bonuses and taxable stock option redemptions, but excluding nontaxable fringe benefits) paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by an employee. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), qualified services consist strictly of engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, engaging in the immediate (first-line) direct supervision of qualified research, or engaging in direct support of qualified research, such as machining a part for an experimental model or compiling research data, while excluding general administrative services like payroll, accounting, or janitorial work. Supervision by higher-level executives to whom first-line managers report is excluded unless those executives personally perform hands-on research or direct first-line supervision, as examined in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201. Under the "substantially all" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80 percent of an employee's wages during the taxable year (allocated by time spent) are for qualified services, then 100 percent of that employee's wages for the taxable year qualify as in-house QREs.

The second and third in-house categories cover supplies and computer use under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)–(iii). Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b), supplies include any tangible property consumed directly in the performance of qualified services, explicitly excluding land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. General utility charges—such as water, electricity, and natural gas—are excluded as general and administrative expenses unless the taxpayer establishes extraordinary additional utility expenditures required by the special character of the research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii). IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4) also include amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use time-sharing or cloud computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user.

The fourth category consists of contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e), which generally equal 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of qualified research, or services that would constitute qualified services if performed by an employee. Statutory exceptions increase this inclusion rate to 75 percent for payments to a qualified research consortium under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100 percent for payments to eligible small businesses, universities, or Federal laboratories for qualified energy research under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D).
The Statutory Four-Part Test Under IRC § 41(d)

To constitute "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2), research activities must satisfy all four components of the statutory Four-Part Test, applied separately to each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A). The first statutory requirement is the Section 174A / Section 174 Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), which mandates that the expenditures qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (or IRC § 174 for pre-2025 tax years). Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent R&D costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense" if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product, or the appropriate design of that product.

The second statutory requirement is the Discovering Technological Information Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii), (a)(3), and (a)(4), which requires that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information "if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component" regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it "fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science".

The third statutory requirement is the Business Component Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(2), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii), under which the taxpayer must intend that the application of the discovered information be useful in the development of a new or improved "business component" of the taxpayer—defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component that must independently satisfy the Four-Part Test.

The fourth statutory requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test for a Qualified Purpose under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), § 41(d)(3), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(iii), (a)(5), and (a)(6), which mandates that "substantially all" of the research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the IRS ATG, a process of experimentation requires three core evaluative steps: identifying the uncertainty regarding the development or improvement of the business component; identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and identifying and conducting a process of evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Finally, under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), a "qualified purpose" (often termed the Permitted Purpose requirement) means the research relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, and IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) expressly disqualifies research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

Practitioners frequently reorganize the statutory requirements into four functional headings (Permitted Purpose, Technological in Nature, Elimination of Uncertainty, and Process of Experimentation, treating Business Component as the object of the tests), whereas the statute (IRC § 41(d)(1)) and the IRS ATG (June 2005) structure the four tests as the Section 174/174A test, the Discovering Technological Information test, the Business Component test, and the Process of Experimentation for a Qualified Purpose test.

Strike Tax asserts that under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), an issued patent "automatically satisfies three of the four elements of the 4-Part Test (Purpose, Technological, and Eliminating Uncertainty)". Under the hierarchy of legal authorities, the statute (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)) and Treasury regulations (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)) carry controlling legal weight over consultancy commentary. The plain text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) applies solely to IRC § 41(d) and paragraph (a)(3)(i)—conclusively establishing only that the taxpayer "has discovered information that is technological in nature that is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component". It does not conclusively establish the qualified purpose requirement (IRC § 41(d)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)), the 80 percent process of experimentation requirement (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and (a)(6)), or the taxpayer's business component nexus (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)).
Definitive Analysis of the Patent Safe Harbor Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)
Regulatory Text, History, and Statutory Citations

The Patent Safe Harbor is codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), which provides in full: "For purposes of section 41(d) and paragraph (a)(3)(i) of this section, the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 151 (other than a patent for design issued under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 171) is conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature that is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. However, the issuance of such a patent is not a precondition for credit availability".

The regulatory history of this provision clarifies why its scope is deliberately narrow. Following the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. 99-514, 100 Stat. 2085), Treasury initially issued final regulations in T.D. 8930 (66 FR 290, Jan. 3, 2001) requiring that "discovering information" obtain knowledge that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field. When Treasury subsequently proposed and finalized T.D. 9104 (69 FR 26, Jan. 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, per 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e)), it abandoned the "common knowledge" discovery threshold, aligning § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) with the § 1.174-2(a)(1) elimination-of-uncertainty standard. During rulemaking for T.D. 9104, public commentators requested that the Patent Safe Harbor in § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) be expanded to cover additional elements of qualified research, including the process of experimentation requirement. In the preamble to T.D. 9104, the Treasury Department and the IRS expressly rejected those requests, stating that "the Treasury Department and the IRS continue to believe that the patent safe harbor is appropriately limited and, therefore, have not changed the patent safe harbor provision".

Both the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (June 2005, Section 3, "Patent Safe Harbor") and the Strike Tax commentary (August 13, 2026) state that the Patent Safe Harbor applies to the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under "35 U.S.C. § 51" (or "35 USC sections 51"). In addition, Strike Tax misprints the C.F.R. citation as "26 C.F.R. § 41-4(a)(3)(iii)". The authoritative text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) in the Code of Federal Regulations and T.D. 9104 confirms that both are typographical errors: the regulation is 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) and the patent issuance statute is 35 U.S.C. § 151 ("Issue of patent: If it appears that applicant is entitled to a patent under the law, a written notice of allowance of the application shall be given or mailed to the applicant... Upon payment of this sum the patent shall issue").
Exclusion of Design Patents (35 U.S.C. § 171) Versus Utility Patents

Title 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) expressly carves out "a patent for design issued under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 171" from the Patent Safe Harbor. Under 35 U.S.C. § 171(a) (in force as of September 16, 2026) and Section 1501 of the USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP, updated March 9, 2026), a design patent may be obtained by "[w]hoever invents any new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture". Whereas a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 101 protects the functional and technical composition, machine, manufacture, or process ("how it works"), a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171 protects ornamental appearance, shape, configuration, or surface ornamentation ("how something looks"), and a design dictated solely by function is not ornamental.

This regulatory exclusion in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) directly reinforces IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), which mandate that research shall in no event be treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors". The Tax Court's decision in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, illustrates this boundary in practice: although the court held that 11 of Estech Systems, Inc.'s (ESI) 12 representative hardware and software telephone system projects constituted qualified research, it disallowed the twelfth project (Chameleon)—which incorporated a third-party skinning tool so users could alter the visual look and feel of the graphical user interface—because resolving technical uncertainty purely for cosmetic or aesthetic interface customization lacked a qualified functional purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3).
Patent Not a Precondition and Correction of the "Novelty" Misconception

The final sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) states that "the issuance of such a patent is not a precondition for credit availability". Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) establishes two critical rules for unpatented or patent-pending research: first, a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering technological information "does not require the taxpayer be seeking to obtain information that exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering in which the taxpayer is performing the research"; and second, discovering technological information "does not require that the taxpayer succeed in developing a new or improved business component".

Second, a taxpayer filing a standard R&D credit claim under IRC § 41(d) is not required to prove that its research was "novel" in the patent-law sense (35 U.S.C. §§ 101–103), because T.D. 9104 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) explicitly abolished the industry-wide "discovery / common knowledge" requirement in 2004. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), a taxpayer need only establish that the information available to the taxpayer did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving the business component. Because obtaining a utility patent from the USPTO requires demonstrating statutory novelty and non-obviousness over prior art (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 103, 151)—a substantially higher threshold than taxpayer-specific technical uncertainty—the IRS accepts an issued utility patent as a fortiori conclusive proof that the taxpayer satisfied 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i).
Timing Discrepancies, Shrinking-Back Nexus, and Cost Segregation

Three operational rules govern how taxpayers deploy the Patent Safe Harbor and account for patent-related expenditures across multi-year product development cycles. The first rule addresses the retrospective timing of patent issuance: as the IRS ATG (June 2005) instructs examiners, "the securing of a patent usually occurs sometime after the actual research year(s)" in which the underlying QREs were paid or incurred. In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, for example, CEO Eric Suder and CTO Buzz Hansen were named as inventors on 13 patents whose application dates predated or postdated the 2004–2007 tax years at issue, alongside one patent reissuance filed on June 3, 2005. Because USPTO prosecution frequently spans multiple years after the tax return for the credit year is filed, the Patent Safe Harbor primarily operates retrospectively during an IRS examination or administrative appeal to conclusively validate 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) for the earlier research years.

The second operational rule governs Business Component nexus and the shrinking-back rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2). The conclusive presumption of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) attaches only to the specific business component—or discrete subset of elements—covered by the issued patent claims. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1)–(2), the Four-Part Test applies first at the level of the overall business component offered for sale, lease, license, or used in the taxpayer's business. If the overall product or system fails to meet the Four-Part Test (for example, fails the 80 percent "substantially all" process-of-experimentation threshold across the entire product), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) (the shrinking-back rule) directs that the requirements be applied to the "most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention" and continue shrinking back until a discrete subcomponent (such as a patented carburetor within a modified motorcycle engine, per 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3), Example) satisfies all requirements. However, as demonstrated in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024, a taxpayer can invoke the shrinking-back rule for a discrete subcomponent only if its time tracking and cost accounting records (26 CFR § 1.41-4(d)) permit isolating the wages and supplies attributable to that specific subcomponent.

The third operational rule mandates strict segregation of patent procurement and legal costs between 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and IRC § 41(b). While technical documentation generated during patent preparation (specifications, drawings, prior art distinctions, and inventor logs) serves as valuable substantiation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), the financial costs of obtaining a patent must be segregated from QREs. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) (T.D. 6500, as amended by T.D. 9680, 79 FR 42195, July 21, 2014), research or experimental expenditures under section 174 (and section 174A) explicitly include "the costs of obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application". However, under IRC § 41(b) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2, patent attorney fees, USPTO filing fees, and administrative IP protection costs are not wages for qualified services, supplies used in conducting research, or contract research expenses for performing qualified experimentation; they are therefore ineligible for the IRC § 41 tax credit. In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, Senior VP Harvey Wende testified that certain claimed contract research expenses were paid to two law firms for "patent research and patent prosecution," and the Tax Court allowed those expenses by citing 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) without analyzing whether legal patent prosecution services satisfied the exclusive QRE definition of IRC § 41(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e). Legal commentators and IRS guidance note that Suder contained no statutory analysis on this point, and the IRS QRE Audit Techniques Guide (July 2, 2026) strictly enforces the rule that expenses not enumerated in IRC § 41(b)—including legal, administrative, and royalty/license expenses—must be excluded from QRE calculations.

body.text: The Compliance Trap: Interaction Between the Patent Safe Harbor and Funded Research Rules
The Activity-Expense Disconnect and Statutory/Regulatory Citation Corrections

The most severe compliance trap surrounding the Patent Safe Harbor occurs when patented research is performed under a client contract, joint venture, or government grant. Even when a USPTO utility patent conclusively establishes that the technical work satisfied 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), the taxpayer cannot claim any R&D tax credit if the research is excluded as "funded research".

In Title 26 of the United States Code, 26 U.S.C. § 41(e) is titled "Credit allowable with respect to certain payments to qualified organizations for basic research" (governing corporate payments to universities and scientific organizations for basic research under IRC § 41(a)(2)); the statutory exclusion for funded research is actually codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). Similarly, in Title 26 of the Code of Federal Regulations, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e) is titled "Effective dates" (specifying that § 1.41-4 applies to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003). The regulatory exclusion for funded research is located at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9) ("Research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise"), which states: "Qualified research does not include any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity). To determine the extent to which research is so funded, § 1.41-4A(d) applies". Consequently, the operative regulatory standards governing funded research are codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(6) (as well as 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3) for research performed for others and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) for contract research expenses).
The Dual Standards of Non-Funded Research Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1) (current as of November 9, 2026), all agreements—not only formal research contracts—entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons (including governmental entities) must be examined to determine the extent to which the research is funded. For a performing taxpayer's research to be completely unfunded and 100 percent eligible for QRE treatment, the taxpayer must satisfy two cumulative standards: the Economic Risk Standard and the Substantial Rights Standard.
The Economic Risk Standard Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1), research is funded to the extent the performing taxpayer is entitled to payment regardless of whether the research succeeds. Conversely, "[a]mounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding". In the foundational decision Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), where an aircraft manufacturer contracted with the U.S. Air Force under a fixed-price incentive contract to design and produce the T-46A trainer aircraft, the Federal Circuit held that the sole inquiry in assigning financial risk is which party bears the research costs in the event of technical failure. Because the contract obligated the Air Force to pay only if Fairchild delivered prototypes meeting over 1,000 pages of detailed technical specifications upon formal inspection—and required Fairchild to refund bimonthly progress advances if it failed to deliver conforming results—Fairchild bore the economic risk, rendering the research unfunded.

Subsequent appellate and trial decisions have reinforced that contract pricing labels alone do not establish economic risk. In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), the Eleventh Circuit held that while fixed-price contracts containing explicit client inspection, acceptance, and rejection criteria tied to research success placed economic risk on the researcher, "capped" time-and-materials contracts (billing labor and expenses up to a maximum ceiling) lacked rejection mechanisms contingent on technical success and were therefore disqualified as funded research. The court emphasized that the business risk of exceeding a budget or losing contract profitability does not constitute economic risk of research failure under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Likewise, in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2024, affirming the Tax Court), the Eighth Circuit denied approximately $190,000 in R&D credits claimed for structural engineering designs (tax years 2010, 2011, and 2013), holding that fixed-price phased contracts adhering to general professional standards of care or building codes constitute "proper performance," which is legally distinct from "successful performance" contingent on resolving technical uncertainty. Similarly, in Perficient Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 15467-17 (Tax Ct. July 11, 2022) and Grigsby v. United States, No. 19-00596-BAJ-SDJ (M.D. La. Oct. 19, 2022), courts confirmed that payments conditioned merely on the passage of time or lacking detailed technical acceptance specifications fail the economic risk test.
The Substantial Rights Standard Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3)

Even when a performing taxpayer bears 100 percent of the economic risk, 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) mandates that "[i]f a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded for purposes of section 41(d)(4)(H), and no expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer in performing the research are qualified research expenses". If an agreement "confers on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research," the performing taxpayer retains no substantial rights and the research is fully funded under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Furthermore, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), "[a] taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research". However, in Lockheed Martin Corporation v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), the Federal Circuit rejected the government's contention that substantial rights require exclusive ownership, holding that Lockheed retained substantial rights because it preserved the non-exclusive right to use the research results and manufacture similar products in its own business without paying the government for that right. Likewise, in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 405-17 (Tax Ct. 2020), the Tax Court ruled on summary judgment that an architectural firm retained substantial rights even though clients owned the specific project models, because no contract provision restricted Populous from reusing the underlying research technology in future projects or required it to pay clients to do so.

By contrast, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2), "[i]ncidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". In Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), and Grigsby v. United States (M.D. La. 2022), courts held that general engineering know-how or skills acquired during contract performance are mere incidental benefits, and that "work for hire" clauses or broad assignment provisions transferring "all rights, title, and interest" or all inventions and discoveries to the client strip the contractor of substantial rights. In Perficient Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 15467-17, the taxpayer challenged the procedural and substantive validity of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2)'s substantial-rights standard under the Administrative Procedure Act and Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, a question further spotlighted by the Supreme Court's decision overturning Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), though 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) remains the regulation in force.

Two additional regulatory mechanisms in 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3) govern split-risk and partial-funding arrangements. First, the final sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) establishes a "whipsaw" disqualification rule: "If a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research and if the payments to the researcher are contingent upon the success of the research, neither the performer nor the person paying for the research is entitled to treat any portion of the expenditures as qualified research expenditures". In that scenario, the performer is disqualified under § 1.41-4A(d)(2) for lacking substantial rights, while the payor is disqualified under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) because its payment is contingent on success (and thus paid for a product or result rather than for the performance of contract research). Second, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)–(ii), if the performing taxpayer does retain substantial rights in the research, but receives non-contingent funding payments that are less than its total research expenditures, the taxpayer generally reduces its otherwise qualified research expenses dollar-for-dollar by the amount of funding under § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i). However, if the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the IRS that the total amount of research expenses is known, that total research expenses exceed the funding, and that the otherwise qualified research expenses exceed 65 percent of the funding, then 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) permits the taxpayer to allocate the funding pro rata between nonqualified and otherwise qualified research expenses—provided that in no event shall less than 65 percent of the funding be applied against the otherwise qualified research expenses.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Semiconductor Fabrication (ChipCo and FabCorp)

Assume ChipCo, a U.S. semiconductor design firm, enters into a written contract with FabCorp, an unrelated U.S. specialized semiconductor fabrication facility, prior to the performance of research. FabCorp's engineers and scientists perform uncertain extreme-ultraviolet lithography and chemical vapor deposition experiments in the United States to fabricate a novel 3D transistor structure designed by ChipCo. The USPTO issues a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151 covering the novel chip structure and fabrication method. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), this utility patent is conclusive evidence that the underlying research discovered information that is technological in nature and intended to eliminate technical uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and (a)(4). Assume both parties independently substantiate the remaining IRC § 41(d) requirements (Business Component nexus, ≥ 80% Process of Experimentation, and Qualified Purpose). During the taxable year, FabCorp incurs $1,000,000 in total domestic project costs: $800,000 in taxable Form W-2 wages for U.S. engineers spending 100 percent of their time directly engaging in and supervising the lithography experimentation (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d)), $150,000 in non-depreciable silicon wafers and specialty chemical supplies consumed in fabricating experimental pilot models (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)), and $50,000 in general and administrative overhead (26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)). Thus, FabCorp's otherwise eligible in-house QREs equal:
FabCorp Eligible In-House QREs = $800,000 + $150,000 = $950,000

while the $50,000 overhead is nonqualified. Separately, ChipCo pays $40,000 to an outside patent law firm to draft and prosecute the U.S. utility patent application; under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and IRC § 174A, this $40,000 qualifies as a deductible domestic R&E expenditure under IRC § 174A, but $0 (0%) qualifies as a QRE under IRC § 41(b).

Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1), the 65 percent reduction applies only to contract research expenses paid by a hiring taxpayer (ChipCo) to an outside contractor. When FabCorp's research is unfunded (26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)) and FabCorp retains substantial rights (26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2)), FabCorp claims its own in-house research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)) at 100 percent ($950,000), not 65 percent ($617,500). Recomputing the exact eligible QREs for both FabCorp and ChipCo across four distinct contractual structures illustrates the precise mathematical and legal outcomes.

In Scenario A, representing unfunded research in which FabCorp bears economic risk and retains substantial rights, ChipCo agrees to pay FabCorp $1,200,000 strictly contingent upon FabCorp delivering working prototypes that pass formal post-inspection technical benchmarks under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1), and while ChipCo owns the chip layout IP, FabCorp retains a royalty-free, non-exclusive license to use the patented fabrication techniques in its business for other commercial clients under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3). Because payment is contingent on technical success and FabCorp retains substantial rights, the research is unfunded. FabCorp claims 100 percent of its in-house QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2):
FabCorp QREs (Scenario A) = $800,000 + $150,000 = $950,000

Conversely, because ChipCo's $1,200,000 payment is contingent on the success of the research, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) treats the payment as paid for a product or result rather than for the performance of contract research; including 0% of the $40,000 patent legal fees, ChipCo's eligible QREs equal $0 (0%).

In Scenario B, representing funded contract research performed on behalf of ChipCo in which ChipCo bears economic risk and acquires exclusive rights, ChipCo pays FabCorp $1,200,000 on a non-contingent cost-reimbursement or fixed-schedule basis regardless of whether the research succeeds under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), and the contract vests exclusive ownership of all resulting inventions and fabrication techniques in ChipCo under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Assume 95 percent of ChipCo's $1,200,000 payment ($1,140,000) is attributable to qualified services performed by FabCorp under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1). Because FabCorp bears no economic risk and retains no substantial rights, the research is fully funded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2), so FabCorp's eligible QREs equal $0 (0%). Because the written agreement was entered into prior to the research, the research was performed on ChipCo's behalf, and ChipCo bore the expense even if unsuccessful, ChipCo satisfies the three-part test of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) and claims 65 percent of the $1,140,000 paid for qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A):
ChipCo QREs (Scenario B) = 0.65 × $1,140,000 = $741,000
in contract research QREs, while the $40,000 patent procurement fees remain $0.

In Scenario C, illustrating the "whipsaw" disqualification trap under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) where FabCorp bears economic risk but ChipCo acquires exclusive rights, ChipCo's $1,200,000 payment is strictly contingent upon FabCorp successfully delivering working prototypes meeting technical specifications (so FabCorp bears 100 percent of the economic risk), but the contract assigns all IP rights exclusively to ChipCo (or requires FabCorp to pay a license fee to ChipCo to use the derived fabrication techniques). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (d)(3)(i), because FabCorp retains no substantial rights (or must pay to use the results), the research is treated as fully funded regardless of FabCorp's economic risk, making FabCorp's eligible QREs $0 (0%). Simultaneously, under the explicit whipsaw rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), because ChipCo's payment is contingent upon the success of the research, ChipCo cannot treat any portion of the $1,200,000 payment as a contract research expense, making ChipCo's eligible QREs $0 (0%)—meaning $950,000 of genuine, patented research expenses yields zero credit for either taxpayer.

In Scenario D, representing partially funded research with substantial rights retained under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3), FabCorp retains substantial non-exclusive rights to use the patented fabrication techniques royalty-free in its business, and ChipCo pays FabCorp $600,000 in non-contingent funding (payable regardless of success), while FabCorp absorbs all remaining costs above $600,000 ($1,000,000 total research expenses, of which $950,000 are otherwise eligible QREs and $50,000 are nonqualified expenses). Under the default rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), FabCorp reduces its $950,000 of otherwise eligible QREs by 100 percent of the $600,000 funding ($950,000 − $600,000 = $350,000). However, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii), because FabCorp's total research expenses ($1,000,000) exceed the funding ($600,000) and its otherwise eligible QREs ($950,000) exceed 65 percent of the funding (0.65 × $600,000 = $390,000), FabCorp may allocate the $600,000 funding pro rata to its otherwise eligible QREs:
which exceeds the $390,000 65 percent statutory floor, yielding:
FabCorp Net Eligible QREs (Scenario D) = $950,000 − $570,000 = $380,000

in net eligible QREs for FabCorp. Assuming the written contract satisfies 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) and 95 percent of ChipCo's $600,000 non-contingent payment ($570,000) is attributable to qualified services, ChipCo claims:
ChipCo Contract QREs (Scenario D) = 0.65 × $570,000 = $370,500
in contract research QREs under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A).

body.text: Grounded Analysis: Administrative, Regulatory, and Compliance Takeaways
Administrative and Regulatory Reform Proposals

Under current law, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) ("Recordkeeping for the research credit") already authorizes the IRS and taxpayers to "agree to guidelines for the keeping of specific records for the purpose of substantiating research credits". Following the January 10, 2022 IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum imposing stricter administrative substantiation requirements for R&D credit refund claims, formal guidance mapping patent application disclosures to the remaining IRC § 41(d) prongs would align with 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) without requiring statutory amendment.

Given the confusion created by Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201—where the Tax Court allowed contract payments to two patent law firms by citing 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) without analyzing IRC § 41(b)(3)—and the enactment of IRC § 174A in Pub. L. 119-21 (effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), explicit IRS guidance confirming where engineering experimentation ends and legal patent prosecution begins would reduce examination disputes. Similarly, because federal appellate precedent (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366) already establishes that substantial rights do not require exclusivity, codifying concrete contractual examples in administrative guidance would curb audit controversies over standard government and commercial IP clauses.

As documented in T.D. 9104 (69 FR 26, Jan. 2, 2004), Treasury and the IRS previously rejected commentator requests to expand 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) beyond paragraph (a)(3)(i). Until any statutory or regulatory amendment is enacted, taxpayers must contemporaneously document the Four-Part Test in the tax year the QREs are incurred (26 CFR § 1.41-4(d)) rather than relying on a future patent grant to excuse missing process-of-experimentation or business-component records.
Taxpayer Compliance and Audit Defense Protocols

First, taxpayers must cross-reference patent claims to specific business components under IRC § 41(d)(2) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2). Practitioners should map each issued utility patent (and pending nonprovisional application) to the exact product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention claimed as a business component in the relevant tax years. Where a patent covers a discrete subsystem (such as a hydraulic feedback loop within an assembly arm or a specific encryption protocol within a software suite), taxpayers must maintain component-level time and cost tracking so the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) can be applied without failing on substantiation as occurred in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024.

Second, taxpayers must apply verified judicial precedent—specifically Suder v. Commissioner, not Sudderth. Denise Sudderth v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Docket No. 37021-21 (U.S. Tax Court, Feb. 14, 2022, Chief Judge Maurice B. Foley), is a two-paragraph procedural order designating Memphis, Tennessee, as the place of trial due to a missing form, with zero connection to patents or IRC § 41 (and Sudderth v. Commissioner of Social Security Administration, Case No. 4:09cv513, E.D. Tex., is a Social Security case). The actual Tax Court decisions governing R&D credit documentation, patent evidence, and the process of experimentation are Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (evaluating 12 representative projects of a company holding 13 patents and 1 patent reissuance, validating structured iterative hardware/software engineering as a process of experimentation while disallowing cosmetic GUI skinning under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)), Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235 (addressing patent evidence and documentation of experimentation under IRC § 41), and Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37 (emphasizing contemporaneous documentation of the three-element process of experimentation across all claimed tax years).

Third, taxpayers must contemporaneously document the 80 percent process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6). Because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) does not prove that a process of experimentation occurred, engineering teams must retain contemporaneous engineering records—such as version-control/git logs, laboratory notebooks, CAD/simulation iterations, prototype test failure logs, and technical design review minutes—demonstrating how alternatives were systematically evaluated to resolve the uncertainty later memorialized in the patent.

Fourth, corporate legal and tax teams must standardize R&D contract clauses to prevent Funded Research disqualification under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d). Before executing customer, joint-venture, or government R&D contracts, IP counsel and tax counsel should coordinate review to ensure that if the performing company intends to claim in-house QREs, payments are explicitly contingent on passing detailed technical acceptance specifications (with client rejection and refund remedies for technical failure, per Fairchild Industries and Geosyntec) and the performing company retains royalty-free substantial rights to use the resulting technology in its business (avoiding "work for hire" or exclusive assignment clauses, per Lockheed Martin, Dynetics, and Grigsby); or, conversely, if the hiring company intends to claim 65 percent contract research QREs under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), the written agreement is signed prior to the research and obligates the hiring company to bear the research costs even if the research fails—thereby avoiding the 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) whipsaw trap.
